cards.title: Richard M. Smith
cards.prompt: One weekend in March 1999 a Cambridge, Massachusetts software executive read a number out of the Melissa Word file. What number, and what did he compare it against to produce a suspect?
cards.answer: The Ethernet (MAC) address sitting inside the document's GUID. He compared it against older virus files posted by a writer calling himself VicodinES, found the same address, and turned the lead over to the FBI.
cards.body: Smith, 45, ran Phar Lap Software. Earlier that month he had gone public about the hardware numbers Office 97 writes into every document. When Melissa spread, he read the same number out of the virus file: "I started looking for files which contained the same Ethernet address." By Sunday he had a match.

cards.title: Melissa
cards.sub: 26 March 1999 · a macro virus riding a Word 97 document
cards.prompt: Melissa's Word document carried a fingerprint of the machine that made it. What figure did its author's federal plea agreement put the damage at, and what did the sentence come to?
cards.answer: More than $80 million in damage, acknowledged by David L. Smith in a cooperating federal plea agreement. Sentence: 20 months in federal prison, three years of supervised release, and a $5,000 fine.
cards.body: Confirmed reports came in on Friday, March 26, 1999; by Monday the virus sat on more than 100,000 computers at more than 300 organizations. David L. Smith of Aberdeen Township, New Jersey pleaded guilty on 9 December 1999 and was sentenced on 1 May 2002.

cards.title: RFC 4122, §4.1.6 and §4.5
cards.prompt: A version-1 UUID has 48 bits it did not generate. Where do those bits come from, and what price does RFC 4122 quote for obtaining such a number honestly instead?
cards.answer: They are an IEEE 802 MAC address, usually the host's own. §4.5 says the alternative is to apply to the IEEE for your own block of addresses — 'the cost was US$550' — or to use 47 cryptographic-quality random bits with the multicast bit set.
cards.body: Leach, Mealling and Salz: "For UUID version 1, the node field consists of an IEEE 802 MAC address, usually the host address." §4.5 offers the escapes. §6 warns: "Do not assume that UUIDs are hard to guess; they should not be used as security capabilities."

cards.title: The MAC gets ruled out
cards.sub: 1999 and 2024 · Microsoft Office Update, then the IETF
cards.prompt: The leak drew two fixes, twenty-five years apart. What did Microsoft ship in 1999, and which UUID field did the IETF finally rule against — with what handed back in its place?
cards.answer: Microsoft shipped the Office 97 Unique Identifier Patch plus a removal tool for existing files, and dropped the feature from Office 2000. RFC 9562 rules the MAC-derived node field out; UUIDv7 fills those trailing bits with randomness and puts a 48-bit millisecond timestamp in front instead — index locality back, creation time disclosed.
cards.body: The patch stopped new Office 97 documents carrying the identifier. Standards took longer. RFC 9562 obsoletes RFC 4122: "MAC addresses pose inherent security risks around privacy and SHOULD NOT be used within a UUID." Exposed addresses locate network interfaces, and virtual machines had broken their uniqueness anyway.
